analysis.one_liner: Requires tax-exempt hospitals to spend at least their full tax exemption's value on community benefits and limits what they can bill charity patients.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House on April 24, 2025, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and has no cosponsors; no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Many hospitals operate as nonprofits and pay little or no federal, state, and local tax in exchange for serving their communities. This bill would tighten that bargain. It would require a tax-exempt hospital to spend, every year, at least as much as the value of its tax exemptions on things like free or discounted care, training, research, and facility improvements — and it could not count buying up physician practices or other hospitals toward that total. It would also require hospitals to bill patients getting financial assistance at Medicare rates instead of higher charges, to treat Medicare and Medicaid patients without limits, and to have community-based boards. It directs government watchdogs to review how hospitals' charity policies work and how well the IRS enforces the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients — especially uninsured and underinsured people — benefit if the bill passes: hospitals would have to bill financial-assistance patients at Medicare rates rather than higher standard charges, and hospitals would have to spend the full value of their tax breaks on care and community benefit each year. Medicare and Medicaid patients would gain a guarantee that hospitals cannot limit how many of them they serve. Taxpayers gain because tax-exempt hospitals would have to deliver benefits worth at least what the public foregoes in taxes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires tax-exempt hospitals to spend at least the dollar value of their federal, state, and local tax exemptions each year on a combination of free or discounted care, training and education, research, and facility improvements.
Bars nonprofit hospitals from counting acquisitions of physician practices, other hospitals, or surgery centers toward that spending requirement.
Requires hospitals to bill patients covered by financial assistance policies at Medicare rates, closing the gap where hospitals charge uninsured or underinsured patients far more.
Requires hospitals to serve Medicare and Medicaid patients without capping how many they see, and to have community-based boards.
Directs the Treasury Inspector General and the Government Accountability Office to review hospital financial assistance policies and IRS enforcement, with annual and recurring reports to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Nonprofit hospital organizations pay: they would face a mandatory annual spending floor equal to their tax exemptions, restrictions on counting acquisitions toward it, and Medicare-rate billing for charity patients. Some of that cost could be passed to commercially insured patients or communities through service changes.

drawbacks.text: The spending requirement counts investments in hospitals' own facilities and equipment (up to half the required amount), so some of the money could flow back into the hospitals' buildings rather than directly to patients in free care.

Banning nonprofit hospitals from buying physician practices and clinics while requiring them to spend their full tax exemption annually could push hospitals to divest from certain communities or slow system growth that some health economists view as improving care coordination.

The bill relies on the IRS to enforce the new standard, and the bill itself directs a review of the IRS's enforcement, acknowledging that current enforcement of hospital charity requirements has been weak.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: nonprofit hospitals receive substantial federal, state, and local tax breaks, and this bill would require them to give back at least that much in charity care, training, and facility investment, plus end the practice of billing uninsured and underinsured patients more than Medicare rates. The costs are the risk that hospitals respond by curtailing services or acquisitions, and that counting facility upgrades toward the requirement lets some of the money flow back to the hospitals' own assets rather than directly to patients. Overall, the patient-facing provisions are substantial and the design is more concrete than most transparency bills, though enforcement would still depend on the IRS, whose past lax enforcement is part of why the bill exists.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it sits with no cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on April 24, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote has been recorded as of the latest action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonprofit hospital systems, which keep their tax exemptions without the new spending floor or billing limits. Patients dealing with hospital bills also get no relief from the status quo.

for.name: Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern has formed.

industries.note: Would face a binding annual spending floor equal to their tax exemptions and lose the ability to count hospital and physician-practice acquisitions as community benefit, directly targeting the dominant business model of large nonprofit systems like CommonSpirit and Ascension. It also ends their ability to charge charity patients more than Medicare rates.

Nonprofit competitors could no longer use their tax advantages to bankroll acquisitions, which could slow consolidation pressure on independent physician practices and for-profit systems. But for-profits are already subject to taxes, so they gain relatively little directly.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action, and no hearing scheduled in a committee with broad jurisdiction and heavy competition for floor time, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress; most single-sponsor bills referred to Ways and Means die there without a markup or vote.
